doc.title: Luis Conte interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 24, 2025

title: Listening to American records in Havana before the embargo
summary: Conte's doctor father loved big bands, Cole and Sinatra and his sister had rock and roll records; all American music stopped with the embargo around 1961.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Were you able to hear American music when you were around 15 or so? I had a conversation with Ignacio Berroa and he talked about trying to pick up American radio
stations and the gymnastics they had to go through with the antennas and all this. And I’m wondering about your experience.

Yeah well two things. One thing, my father was a doctor but he loved music. My whole paternal part of my family was totally musical. None of them are musicians but they all played for fun and they were doctors and professors. And my dad was a doctor and he loved big band music, he loved all kinds of American – I listened to, since I was a yeah little boy I listened to all the big bands, you know Tommy Dorsey etcetera etcetera. And Glenn Miller. He had everything. And up until when the embargo came, after that you couldn’t get any more American records. But -- and he loved Nat King Cole, Sinatra, you know, and my sister, this is just before Castro seized all that remained, so Elvis came along and what was it, Bill Haley and the Comets, she had all these records. Ricky Nelson – I forget now some of the others. Gene Vincent. She had all these records of all these guys. So I grew up listening to the stuff in the house, before the embargo thing happened. This is early – because I was born in ’51 so in ’61 or so, by the time I was ten, that’s when really things got really closed up. So my first ten years I was listening to this music, American music in the house. Then all of a sudden the embargo comes in and we can’t get any more American music and we don’t know what’s going on. We’re totally closed off from the world. And a friend of ours that had left Cuba with his family sent one of my friends a letter with a bubble gum card in it of The Beatles and I will never forget – the letter says, “Hey man, this is what’s happening now. These guys are called The Beatles.” Blah-blah-blah-blah. What is this? You know. So my dad, it just worked out that my dad had just bought a radio, a Russian radio or Czechoslovakian, I don't know where this radio was from. Portable. And I could get, I don't know the station, I never knew, but I would tune in and I would get this station that was in English – I never knew where it came from. I’m from Santiago which is south of the island, southeast. So I don’t think it was Miami or anything up there, it was too far. It could have been Jamaica or I don't know. But it was pop radio. So they played, you know The Beatles, The Stones, Motown music, Aretha Franklin, you know all these, a whole soup of you know the top ten of what was happening. So that’s my American music influence. And honestly, while I was in Cuba I paid more attention to that than our actual traditional thing.
